QF.id: AIFM Modern Portfolio Theory and Capital Market Theory_5

question.text: A wealthy LP in Chenab Opportunities AIF has a risk-aversion index (A) of 4. He is evaluating an AIF sleeve with an expected return of 18% and a return variance (σ²) of 0.04 (i.e. σ = 20%). Using the standard utility function U = E(r) – 0.5·A·σ², what is his utility score?

explanation.text: The Logic: U = E(r) − (1/2)·A·σ². With E(r)=0.18, A=4, σ²=0.04: U = 0.18 − 0.5×4×0.04 = 0.18 − 0.08 = 0.10 = 10%. Utility captures the certainty-equivalent return after penalising variance by the investor's risk-aversion index. The Trap: 16% forgets to subtract the risk-penalty term. 14% uses σ (20%) instead of σ² (4%) in the penalty. 18% is the raw expected return with no risk adjustment. Cross-Exam Context: The utility score appears in X-B (IA L2), XXI-B (PM) and XV (RA). XIX-A/B Distributor exams seldom test the arithmetic but expect the definition. Manager's Pro-Tip: When onboarding a sophisticated LP, document the risk-aversion index you assume in the IPS (Investment Policy Statement). If you structure a fund with leverage beyond the LP's implied 'A', you breach suitability — even before SEBI looks at it.
